**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 15, verse 1:**

[p. 1] **Surah "al-Hijr"**

Its purpose is to describe the Book as being at the summit of gathering the clear meanings of the truth, with no disagreement at all. The most obscure and the most exemplary of what it contains on this theme is the story of the people of al-Hijr. Their sign was clear to them, and to everyone who witnessed it or heard of it, just as what this surah's purpose indicates about the matter of the Book was clear to all the Arabs, especially the Quraysh. Their sign is also entirely clear about the truth and about gathering its meanings, which revolve around monotheism, and this requires unity around the one who calls to it. From here, what I have chosen as the grammatical analysis of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿"As We sent down upon the dividers"﴾ becomes clear and is confirmed. [p. 2] It connects with my linking it to ﴿"so they turned away from it"﴾ [al-Hijr: 81], which requires a strong resemblance between their state in their disbelief and the state of the Quraysh in similar matters, as you will see. Moreover, the word "al-Hijr" indicates what the purpose of the surah indicates: gathering and encircling, whose essence is an encompassing that distinguishes the encompassed from others, with no ambiguity at all. And God knows best.

**"In the name of God"**, the One, the Unique, who gathers what has been scattered into dispersion; **"the Most Merciful"**, who gathered His creation in the mercy of clarification; **"the Most Compassionate"**, who singled out the righteous by granting them what He permitted of approval.

When He concluded the preceding surah with the title of the Book, He began this one by explaining that title. The first part of that explanation is describing it as gathering, for all good lies in gathering and all evil in division. So He said (exalted is He): ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These﴾, that is: these verses of lofty station and precious purpose; ﴿are verses of the Book﴾, that is: the Book perfect in utmost perfection, which in truth has no other book; which gathers all the good by which existence is sustained; which is decisive in its judgment without doubt or hesitation; which prevails with its compelling rulings in its promise, its warning, and its rulings; and which overcomes in its miraculousness everyone who opposes it. [p. 3] Since the dominant theme of this surah is decisiveness, which is one of the necessary attributes of the Book, He put it first. This is because it is decisive regarding the matter of the term, the angels, the preservation of the Book, the hurling of meteors, and the sufficiency against those who mock. So it was as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and﴾ [the verses of] ﴿a Qur'an﴾, that is: a gathering, spreading, detailed, and connected Qur'an, since the tanwin here is for magnification; ﴿clear﴾, regarding all that gathers the resolves upon God so that it leads to happiness. This clarity, which leaves no ambiguity, is characteristic of it together with its being a gathering of the principles and a spreader of the branches; there is no flaw in it through which one may enter against it, nor any breach through which one may attack it. So marvel at a matter that contains gathering, division, separation, and connection.

Clarification (*al-ibana*) means making the meaning manifest to the self by what distinguishes it from other things, because the root of *ibana* is separation. This is the explanation of its being a message (*balagh*). So the purpose of this surah is to affirm that the Qur'an is a comprehensive message containing the matters that lead to God, sufficing in place of all other means, so that one should not turn to anything besides it: ﴿Leave them to eat﴾ [al-Hijr: 3], ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾ [al-Hijr: 88], ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]. The combination of the two descriptions, each of which indicates gathering, is an allusion to refuting them for making the Qur'an into *'idin* (fragments), and that their statement is extremely far from its meaning. [p. 4] Although the two concepts, despite agreeing on one thing, are different: the *kitab* is what is written on pages, and the *Qur'an* is what is recited by the tongue. So the first is like an allusion to its preservation on pages through writing, and the second to its preservation in hearts through study. His saying will come later: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], confirming this. Each of the roots *kataba* and *qara'a*, in all their permutations, revolves around gathering.

As for *kataba*, which turns into *kabata*, *tabaka*, *bakata*, and *batkaa*: in *al-Mujmal* it says: "I wrote the book, I write it," and it is from gathering. *Al-kitab* also means the inkpot, naming a thing by the name of its instrument. *Al-maktab*, like *mu'azzam*, is a cluster of grapes of which some has been eaten, likened to the written. *Al-katiba* is the army, and the group of horses that gathers together when raiding, from a hundred to a thousand; end of quote. *Katabati al-baghla* means when the mule gathers the two lips of its womb with a ring. Al-Qazzaz said: its origin, i.e., of *kitab*, is your joining one thing to another; so it was named thus for joining the letters, some to others. *Katabtu al-mazada* means when I stitched it, [p. 5] i.e., I joined some of it to others.

*Al-kutbah*, with a *damma*, is the strip with which something is stitched, and what is written with it on the female camel's vulva so that it is not mounted. *Al-ikta*b means tightening the head of the waterskin. *Al-katiba* is a group that gathered together, i.e., assembled. *Takabbata al-rajul*, with the *b* placed first, means when he contracted. From this is *al-kuttab*, with a *damma* on the *k* and the upper *t* lightened, for a small arrow with which children learn to shoot. So said al-Qazzaz: it is lightened; in *al-Qamus*: its weight is like *rumman*, and it adds that its head is rounded. *Katabtu al-naqata taktiban* means I tied its vulva. *Iktataba batnuhu* means it held in. *Al-muktawtib* means the filled and the swollen. Gathering entails cutting and dominance, which are necessary for power. From cutting: *al-kitab* in the sense of obligation, judgment, and decree; and *al-batk* is cutting; hence the sword is called *batik*, i.e., cutting. From dominance and power: *al-kitab* in the sense of decree. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-katib* among them is the knowing one; al-Qazzaz said: *al-katib* is the one who preserves. Both of these return also to the very essence of gathering: the gathering of the preserver with the preserved, and of the knower with the known. *Kabata Allahu al-'aduwwa*, with the *b* placed first, means He turned them away humiliated, which comes from *takabbata al-rajul* when he contracted. [p. 6] Al-Qazzaz's expression: "*Kabata a'da'ahu*" means He returned them with their rage, i.e., they were suppressed and gathered back from what they had spread out against him. *Kabata al-rajula* means when he threw him on his face. *Bakkatahu tabkitan* means when he rebuked him, or struck him with a staff, a sword, or the like, because of the diminishment of his self and its contraction that results from it.

As for *qara'a*, with hamza, which turns into *raqa'a*, *araqa*, and *aqara*; and without hamza, with *ya*: its permutations are five: *qarya*, *qayara*, *raqya*, *rayaqa*, *yaraqa*; and with *waw*: its permutations are six: *qarawa*, *qawara*, *raqawa*, *rawaqa*, *waqara*, and *waraqa*. It is also for gathering, and it entails retention, though sometimes spreading is associated with it. From gathering: *qara'tu al-Qur'an*, i.e., I recited it, so I made some of its letters, words, and verses follow some others, connected to them, gathered with them. Recitation entails worship; from it come *al-qari'*, *al-mutaqarri'*, and *al-qurra'* (like *rumman*), i.e., the devout. From it follows jurisprudence; hence it is said *taqarra'a* when one became learned in jurisprudence, and this too is from gathering itself, because the devout gathers worship to recitation and his resolve is gathered, and the jurist gathers jurisprudence to it. In *al-Mujmal* it says: "*al-Qur'an*" is from "*al-qar'*", which is gathering, i.e., in form and meaning. In *al-Qamus*: "*qara'a 'alayhi al-salam*" means he conveyed greetings to him, like *aqra'ahu*; and one does not say *aqra'ahu* except when the greeting was written. [p. 7] Al-Zubaydi said in the abridgment of *al-'Ayn*: "*qara'at al-mar'atu qur'an*" when the woman saw blood, and "*aqra'at*" when she menstruated, so she is *muqri'*; end of quote. It seems he expressed it that way at the sight of blood, because it is not known that the woman gathered it except by seeing it. This is from spreading, which may entail gathering; or *fa'ala* here is for removal, so its meaning is: she removed the retention of the blood, just as this is the meaning of *aqra'at*. For *fa'ala*, because of its lightness and frequency of use, takes on the meanings of all the forms. In *al-Mujmal* it says: "*aqra'at al-mar'a*": she went out from purity to menstruation or from menstruation to purity. I say: the first involves *af'ala* for removal, and the second for entering into something, just as you say *atahama al-rajul* and *anjada*, when he entered Tihama or Najd. He said: "*al-qur'*" is a time that is for purity once and for menstruation once. I say: the first is for gathering itself, and the second because it is the indicator of gathering. He said: its plural is *quru'*; it is said *al-qur'* is purity; this is because the pure woman's blood had gathered and held in her body, so it is from *qarayt al-ma'*, and *qara al-akil al-ta'am fi shidqihi*. The two words may differ, one being hamzated and the other not, [p. 8] and the meaning is one when the root is one. Some hold that *al-qur'* is menstruation. In *al-Qamus*: "*al-qur'*", with a *damma*, is menstruation and purity, opposites, and it has been mentioned how this is derived; and the time, because it contains what is in it; and the rhyme, because it gathers the scattering of verses; its plural is *aqru'* and *quru'*; and the plural of menstruation is *aqra'*. The reason for this seems to be that since the plural of multiplicity is the origin among plurals, because what is meant by the plural itself is multiplicity, so whenever it is greater, it is more deserving of it; since the origin is such, and *al-qur'* in the sense of *al-tuhr* is the origin in the meaning of plurality, it deserved the plural of multiplicity, which is more rooted in plurality. Since *al-qur'* in the sense of *al-hayd* is a branch, it had the plural of paucity, which is a branch in the domain of plurals.

*Aqrat*: she menstruated and became pure. *Aqrati al-riyah*: the winds blew at their time, because their blowing indicates their gathering, like the appearance of menstrual blood. *Qara'a al-shay'*: he gathered it and drew it together. *Al-hamil*: she gave birth, because the appearance of the child is what confirms her gathering it in her womb. *Aqra'*: he returned, drew near, delayed, withdrew, disappeared, and departed. [p. 9] And *tanassaka* like *taqarra'a*; some of it is for affirmation and some for negation. *Al-muqarra'a*, like *mu'azzama*: the woman whose periods are awaited to end, and "*qad quri'at*": she was detained for that. *Aqra' al-shi'r*: its kinds and modes, because it gathers the parts. *Al-qir'ah*, with a *kasra*: plague, because it gathers worry. *Istaqra'a al-jamal al-naqata*: the camel left her to see whether she had conceived or not, from tracing and testing, and this has the meaning of gathering evidence. *Qara'at al-naqatu* when she became pregnant, so she is *qari'*, i.e., she gathered a young one in her belly; and *aqrat* when the water settled in her womb.

From retention: *raqa'a al-dam wa al-damu ruqu'an*, when both stopped. Abu Zayd said: *al-ruqu'*, i.e., with a *fatha*, is what is placed on blood so that it calms; *raqa'a baynahum* means he reconciled, and he corrupted; in the sense of climbing: he ascended, and it is *al-mar'aqa*, which may be vocalized with a *kasra*; *raqa'a al-'araq* means it rose. Some of these are in the sense of gathering, and some in the sense of spreading and height, which may entail it. From retention: *al-ara'q*, which is sleeplessness, because it withholds sleep. *Al-irqan* is a worm that occurs in crops, which seems to cause worry, from which sleeplessness results; it is possible that it is from spreading, which may entail gathering [p. 10]; it is possible that it is from gathering itself, because it gathers worry, and God knows best. In *al-Qamus*: *al-irqan*, with a *kasra*: a reddish tree, henna, saffron, and dragon's blood, as if it were a cause for dwelling upon it by inhaling its scent, or because it gathers one color to another by its dye. *Al-irqan* also: a blight that strikes crops and people, like *al-aranan* with a vowel, and with two *kasras*, with a *fatha* on the hamza and a *damma* on the *ra*. *Al-ara'q*, *al-aranan* with both vowels *fatha*; *al-urag*, like *ghurab*; *al-yaraqan*, with a vowel: these are the best-known diseases by which the color of the body changes greatly to yellow or black. As if that, since it was the cause of sleeplessness, was itself the eloquent sleeplessness. *Zar'un ma'ruq* and *mayruq* means blighted. *Al-uqur*, with two *dammas*: a wide valley filled with brackish plants and waters; it is clear in the sense of gathering. Some of this root's material has passed at the end of Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him, at His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Only men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf: 109]; and the rest of it will come, God willing (exalted is He), in Surah Subhan, at His saying: ﴿and in their ears is deafness﴾ [al-Isra': 46].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 2:

(p-11) When He (glorified be He) described this Qur'an with what He described it with of greatness and of clarity in explaining all the aims—among which is the question of the disbelievers, at the sight of the punishment, for a delay so that they may obey—in His saying (exalted be He): ﴿And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]; it was as if it were said: why did He not make clear to the disbelievers the evil of their end with a clarification that would turn them back? So He (glorified be He), expanding upon His saying ﴿and that they may be warned by it﴾ [Ibrahim: 52], said: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾. By His (exalted be He) using the present tense, He indicated that their wish for this will be very great and repeated; and His placing ﴿rubama﴾ (perhaps/often) before it—usually it is followed by the past tense—informs that it is certain, just as the past that has been realized and occurred is considered certain. ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ means: even if only at some time. The word ﴿wadd﴾ (wish) means desire, which is the forming of the meaning in the soul for enjoyment and the manifestation of the inclination of natures toward it; and it carries a shared meaning between wishing and loving. Al-Rummani said: here it is for wishing, for He specified what they wish for with His saying ﴿if they had been﴾, i.e., a natural state, ﴿Muslims﴾, i.e., deeply rooted in the description of Islam from the beginning of their affair to its end. Al-Rummani said: Islam is giving a thing in a state of soundness, like the cloth's Islam to the one who shortens it, and the child's Islam to the one who teaches him; so Islam (p-12), which is faith, is giving the meaning of truth in the religion through affirmation and acting upon it. End of quote. And what Allah reported has occurred: every one of the Companions who embraced Islam regretted delaying his Islam when they knew the excellence of Islam and saw the virtues of the foremost—as is mentioned in the biographies and the conquests of the lands. And what Allah wills of that will occur on the Day of Resurrection and before it. So the meaning is: if you deny the certainty—in such as His saying ﴿Then those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, delay us..."﴾ [Ibrahim: 44], and so on—that you will turn back from this arrogance and disown these dispositions and aspirations, so that you ask Allah (exalted be He) for obedience; but the opportunity has passed with the arrival of the event of death to another; so there is at least doubt on your part concerning matters that are possible. It is not befitting, then, for the intelligent person to neglect preparing for this possibility. This—I mean the diminution—is the signification of ﴿rubba﴾ (perhaps). Some of them said it may also come for multiplication. Ibn Hisham, in his book "al-Mughni" (the Jamal), said: that is its most common usage; and he cited evidences which, on reflection, do not indicate it; and the saying of one who attributed that to al-Kashshaf is not correct, for its speech is taken from al-Zajjaj. The wording of al-Zajjaj—as the Imam Jamal al-Din Muhammad ibn al-Mukarram transmitted it in his book "Lisan al-Arab," and I transcribed it from his handwriting—is: whoever says that ﴿rubba﴾ is meant for multiplication has opposed what the Arabs know. If someone says: why then is it permitted in His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾, while ﴿rubba﴾ is for diminution? The answer: the Arabs were addressed in what they know in threatening; a man threatens another and says, "Perhaps you will regret your action," while he does not doubt that he will regret; and he says, "Perhaps a person regrets what you have done," while he knows that a person regrets much. But its figurative sense is that if this were of what is wished in one state of the states of punishment, or if a person feared that he would regret something, it would be obligatory for him to avoid it. The proof that it carries the meaning of threat is His saying (exalted be He): ﴿Leave them to eat (p-14) and enjoy themselves﴾ [al-Hijr: 3]. End of quote.

It is known from this that they use it in the sense of fewness regarding what they know to be abundant, as a loosening of the reins and as an alert to the obligation of taking the more cautious course. That occurs in threatening. There is a great difference between what is known to be abundant from a matter outside the expression that reports it, and what its abundance is known from that expression itself. ﴿Ma﴾ has been added to it for emphasis, in that it conveys that the matter cannot be other than thus; and for preparing it for the verb to come after it. Abu Hayyan said: the apparent view is that ﴿ma﴾ in ﴿rubba﴾ is preparatory; because it, as a preposition (according to a difference of opinion), is only followed by nouns; so ﴿ma﴾ was brought to prepare for the verb coming after it. And despite the frequency of ﴿rubba﴾ in Arabic speech, it does not occur in the Qur'an except in this place. End of quote. It is followed here by the present tense, though it is for the past, because of the truth of the promise, as if it were a direct witnessing that has already occurred; or because ﴿ma﴾, when attached to it, permits its entry upon the future, just as it enters upon the definite. Al-Rummani said: (p-15)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 3:

When He, glorified is He, presented to them the possibility, it was as if it were said: Have they accepted it and begun preparing for it? It was answered: Rather, they persisted in their obstinacy. So He said, beginning a new statement, turning to what He had indicated at the beginning of Surat Ibrahim, in His words: ﴿Those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾ [Ibrahim: 3], which is what prevents them from submitting: ﴿Leave them﴾, O most dear of creation to Us, like cattle, ﴿to eat and enjoy themselves﴾. Al-tamattu' (enjoyment) is al-taladhdhudh (taking pleasure), which is the seeking of pleasure moment after moment, just as al-taqarrub (drawing near) is the seeking of nearness moment after moment. ﴿And let hope divert them﴾, that is, let it occupy them from taking their share of happiness. ﴿Hope﴾, that is, their expectation of a long life and of attaining what imagination conceives of as delights, without any cause that prepares for it.

Since this is a matter that only a fool would be occupied with, He made the threat its consequence, in His words: ﴿They will come to know﴾, that is, what will befall them after We granted them a span of time for enjoyment. Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr (d. 708 AH) said in his Burhan (Proof): When the threat against the disbelievers that the verses concluding Surat Ibrahim contained had preceded, from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], to its end, He followed that with His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾ [al-Hijr: 2], that is, when they witness those tremendous circumstances. Then He, exalted is He, said, emphasizing that threat: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope divert them; they will come to know.﴾ Then He, exalted is He, followed this by explaining what He made a established practice among His servants: the linking of reward and punishment, hastened and deferred, at times and moments, with no separation between them and no advance or delay. Hastening the seizing usually comes only from one who fears missing out, whereas the whole world belongs to Allah, exalted is He, and is in His grip; none of them escapes Him, nor can they overpower Him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We never destroyed a town except that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]. This clarifies His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare﴾ [Ibrahim: 42]; and His words: ﴿Warn the people of the Day the punishment will come to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]; and His words: ﴿On the Day the earth will be changed into other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and so on. Reflect on the revelation of His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾ [al-Hijr: 2] in this context, and on its great placement in its connection to what precedes it, and on the clarity of all of that. As for the opening of the surah with His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1], it refers to two clear matters: the first is the proofs and signs that He, glorified is He, pointed out, as is explained; the second is what the glorious Qur'an made clear and explained, and what it contains of proofs and unseen matters, promises and threats, and the confirmation of some of these by others. How then would what is threatened not be in the strength of the event witnessed, given the intensity of the clarity regarding the truth of its occurrence? So how strange is hesitation and denial! Then He followed this with His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾ [al-Hijr: 2]. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 4:

When they were threatened with the verse of enjoyment (tamattu') and the distraction of hope; and it was well known of their condition that they sought to hasten the punishment, in denial and mockery; the speech was in effect such that it would be said: "They said: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, hasten for us what you threaten us with." This was infuriating and painful, and it impelled a wish for swift descent upon them. So the answer was given: "Indeed for them there is a term (ajal) by a Book known (kitab ma'lum); they must reach it, because the one who threatens does not fear escape; he gives respite and does not neglect, for the Word is not changed with Him." So let them prepare, for the matter is unseen, and there is not a moment but that it is fit for punishment to be expected in it. For We do not destroy them except when they reach their known Book. ﴿Wa-ma﴾ (And not): We did not make this specific to them; rather it is Our custom: ﴿ma ahlakna﴾ (We did not destroy) [al-Qasas: 43]; that is, in accordance with the greatness that is Ours. He emphasized the negation, saying: ﴿min qaryatin﴾ (any town); that is, of the towns.

Since the context concerns destruction, their haste, and their mockery of it, and since its decree (taqdir), from Him - glory be to Him - and its Books are from the unseen world, the situation required emphasis with what indicates that it is decreed, settled, and that its decree preceded the time of destruction. So He used the waw, because a circumstantial clause without the waw is like a part of what precedes it, like the predicate and the qualifier, without which the meaning is not complete. The one with the waw is an addition to the preceding statement; therefore the linking by waw was needed, just as it is used for coordination. So He said: ﴿illa wa-laha﴾ (except that for it): that is, while the state is that it has [a term] in its destruction, or for its destruction; ﴿kitab ma'lum﴾ (a known Book): that is, a fixed term, written in the Preserved Tablet. Or the sense may be: "They will know when the punishment comes to them at the term We have written for them whether they will wish for Islam or not."

Then he clarified the preceding verse with his words: ﴿No nation outstrips its term﴾; he emphasized the comprehensiveness with his words: ﴿from a nation﴾; and he made clear that what is meant by the Book is the term, with his words: ﴿its term﴾; that is, the one We have decreed for it; ﴿nor do they delay﴾; that is, they do not delay from it anything at all. He did not say "tastakhiru" (it does not delay), in keeping with the wording, as with the past tense, lest they turn it toward addressing him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, out of obstinate dispute.

Then, when he answered them with this answer, which indicates the perfection of power and the completeness of knowledge, both indicating the oneness (of God), he linked to what had preceded, that it is in the sense of what is uttered, his saying (p-19), indicating their abandoning of the answer in favor of obstinacy and foolishness: ﴿And they said﴾; that is, they did not allow that they would love that; rather they persisted in stubbornness, and said: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾. And since their denial was of the revelation itself, he put into the passive his saying: ﴿has been sent down upon him﴾; that is, according to his claim; ﴿the Reminder﴾. And they made clear that they called it a revelation only in mockery. So they said, emphasizing (what they knew) of their knowledge that their saying was outrageous: ﴿Indeed, you are surely possessed﴾; that is, because of your claim that God sent down to you a reminder, and what you see is a jinn who casts into you confusion. This was evidence of their obstinacy, for they put insult in the place of an answer to what had passed, in the manner of one defeated and cut off in debate.

Having followed up with what they claimed as proof of their position, they said: ﴿Why do you not⁠—﴾ that is, "Why not?" and "What prevents it?" ﴿bring us the angels﴾ as evidence of your truthfulness, either as a witness in your favor or for the destruction of those who oppose you, ﴿if you are﴾ by nature and disposition ﴿of the truthful﴾ in what you say. That is: what is the reason for your being singled out from us for the descent of the angels to you and for your seeing them, when you are like us in humanity, lineage and homeland? This is said after the decisive proofs and the shining demonstrations have established his truthfulness, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, which calls them to a contest at all times and rebukes them with their inability to produce its equal at every moment.

(p-20) Since their statement contained two matters, he answered each of them in the manner of a fresh resumption (istinaf), as if answering a question that might be asked, as though someone had said: "Perhaps then they would be answered." So it is said: he answered the second, because it is closer, with His words: ﴿We do not send down the angels﴾; that is, this kind (of descent), ﴿except﴾ as a descent accompanied by ﴿truth﴾; that is, by means of the enactment of the established decree (amr thabit). This is the meaning of what al-Bukhari said in the Book of Tawhid: Mujahid said: "with the message and the punishment." As for the Messengers, it is with the truth of the statements; and as for those who are warned, it is with the truth of the deeds, from destruction and salvation. ﴿So if they had been sent down to them﴾ - as they demanded - ﴿the matter would have been decided between you and them﴾, and they would have been destroyed. ﴿And they would not have been﴾; that is, the disbelievers; ﴿then﴾; that is, at the time the angels would come to them; ﴿given respite﴾; that is, respite would not have been granted to them under any of the possibilities, because the established decree necessitates the salvation of the obedient and the destruction of the disobedient immediately, without any delay; and at that point what We had decreed concerning their postponement would have been lost, and the bringing forth from their loins of those whose faith We willed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 9:

He - glorified is He - answered the first (objection) with His saying, emphasizing their denial: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder﴾; that is, by virtue of the greatness that belongs to Us, not any other, of jinn or of humans. ﴿Sent down﴾ means gradually, through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him). ﴿The Reminder﴾ means the admonition and the honour. ﴿And indeed, We are its﴾ - that is, by Our greatness, even if the noses of the envious are rubbed in the dust - ﴿guardians﴾; that is, always, by Our power and Our knowledge. This is in accordance with what is in Surah Hud, that such (preservation) is necessarily linked to safeguarding. Thereby the possibility that it could be sent down upon a madman, one confused, is ruled out at that point, especially since (the Reminder) is in these wondrous styles and sublime methods. So the meaning is: We sent you with it while you are a human being, not an angel, strong and sound; they know that you are the most complete of them in intellect, the highest of them in resolve, the most certain of them in thought, the most precise of them in affairs, the most sound of them in opinion, and the firmest of them in determination.

al-Bukhari, in (the books of) Tafsir and Fitan, related from Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) sent for me at the (time of the) killing of the people of Yamamah, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was with him. Abu Bakr said: "'Umar came to me and said: 'Indeed the killing has intensified among the people on the Day of Yamamah' - and in another narration: 'among the reciters of the Qur'an' - 'and I fear that the killing will intensify among the reciters in (other) battlefields, so much of the Qur'an will be lost, unless you collect it. I indeed think that you should collect the Qur'an.'" Abu Bakr said: "I said to 'Umar: 'How can I do something that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not do?' 'Umar said: 'By Allah, it is good.' 'Umar kept returning to me about it until Allah expanded my chest for it, and I saw what 'Umar had seen." Zayd ibn Thabit said: "'Umar was sitting with him, not speaking." Abu Bakr said: "You are a young man, intelligent, and we do not suspect you. You used to write down the revelation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so follow the Qur'an and collect it. By Allah, if he had charged me with moving one of the mountains, it would not have been heavier upon me than what he commanded me concerning the collection of the Qur'an." I said: "How will you two do something that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not do?" Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, it is good." I kept returning to him until Allah expanded my chest for that which He had expanded the chest of Abu Bakr and 'Umar for. So I stood up and tracked down the Qur'an, collecting it from the scraps, the shoulder-blades, the palm-stalks, and the breasts of men, until I found two verses of Surah al-Tawbah with Khuzaymah - or Abu Khuzaymah - al-Ansari, which I did not find with anyone else: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] to its end." The pages on which the Qur'an was collected were with Abu Bakr until Allah (Most High) took him, then with 'Umar until Allah took him, then with Hafsah bint 'Umar - may Allah be pleased with them.

He also cited this report in the section on the virtues of the Qur'an. After it, it is related from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (may Allah be pleased with him) came to 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) - he was fighting with the people of Syria in the conquest of Armenia and Azerbaijan together with the people of Iraq - and the differences among them in recitation alarmed Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him). Hudhayfah said to 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with both of them): "O Commander of the Faithful, save this Ummah before they differ over the Book as the Jews and Christians differed." So 'Uthman sent to Hafsah (may Allah be pleased with both of them): "Send us the pages, and we will copy them into the codices, then we will return them to you." Hafsah sent them to 'Uthman, and he commanded Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-'As, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham (may Allah be pleased with them), and they copied them into the codices. 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) said to the three Qurayshi men: "If you and Zayd ibn Thabit differ over anything in the Qur'an, write it in the language of Quraysh, for it was revealed in their language." They did so. When they had copied the pages into the codices, 'Uthman returned the pages to Hafsah, and he sent to every region a codex of what they had copied, and he commanded that whatever else of the Qur'an existed, in every page or codex, be burned.

Also from Kharijah ibn Zayd ibn Thabit, who heard Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) say: "When we copied the pages into the codices, a verse from Surah al-Ahzab was lost. I used to hear the Messenger (ﷺ) recite it often. I did not find it with anyone except Khuzaymah al-Ansari" - and in another narration: "We searched for it and found it with Khuzaymah, whose testimony the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made equal to the testimony of two men: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23]. So we added it to its surah in the codex."

In the first report there is evidence that when al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) commanded him, he wrote nothing except when he found what had been written in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) and by his command, and he also checked it against what was preserved in the breasts of men. In the last report, there is evidence from his saying "we copied the codex into the codices" to its end, that he repeated the tracking as he had first done, so that his statement "a verse from Surah al-Ahzab was lost" would be valid.

Because the loss of it is a branch of knowing it, and it is most unlikely that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite it often and did not memorize it, especially since he is mentioned among those who collected the Qur'an during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), as al-Bukhari related through several chains from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him). What is apparent from such tracking, which does not permit one who has practised such high aspirations to allow others to understand that he would only transmit a verse if he found it with its memorizers in the number of mass transmission (tawatur) as it is written, is... and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 10:

When this speech that they uttered against him (ﷺ) was grievous and a painful vexation to him, He (Exalted is He) said, as consolation for him and in a manner that repudiates them: ﴿And We had certainly sent﴾; that is, by virtue of the greatness, majesty and awe that belong to Us. Since sending in actuality was not general to the whole of time, He said: ﴿before you﴾; that is, many messengers; ﴿among the sects﴾; that is, groups. They were called shi'a (sects) because some of them followed others in the affairs upon which they gathered in a single era, such as a kingdom, a civilization, a religion, or similar matters that are customary; ﴿of the former peoples﴾, all of them. So We sent none but men from among the people of the towns, like you, to whom We revealed; and We did not send with any of them angels that their peoples could see. Rather, We made the unveiling of the angels a matter specific to the messengers. Then they denied their messengers.

﴿And there does not come to them﴾: he used the present tense to depict the situation, indicating what necessitates anger. For "mā" (not) makes the present tense express a state, and brings the past close to it. He emphasized the negation, saying: ﴿any messenger﴾, meaning: in whatever manner he came; ﴿but they used to mock him﴾, meaning: by their nature and disposition; ﴿mocking﴾, repeating this constantly. It is as if they had counseled one another to do this. This did not diminish Our greatness in any way, so do not grieve over what they do to you. The word "istihza'" (mockery), originally means seeking derision (al-huzu'), and what is meant here, God knows best, is derision (al-huz'), which is displaying what is intended as a defect while giving the appearance of praise, like play and ridicule. Perhaps he expressed it with the "sin" that conveys seeking, to indicate that their desire for it does not end, as is the case with one who seeks something. Yet they never actually attain their aim regarding the people of God, because whatever act of this kind they perform is clearly far from what they intend, due to the evident nature of what the party of God calls to and its steadfastness. Thus they were like one seeking something that never happens (p-27). People are quicker to what ignorance necessitates, such as mockery and the like, than to what knowledge necessitates, namely taking firm resolve (al-hazm) and considering the consequences, because in the former there is the hastening of comfort and pleasure and the removal of hardship, by not obliging the soul to move from one state to another. This was said by al-Rummani.

Since the hearts of the people of misguidance are described as narrow and constricted, whoever enters them can only do so with the utmost difficulty. Therefore, [the verse] says, in answer to one who seems to ask, "Is this specific to them?": "No, rather"—﴿Thus﴾; that is, like this strange and wondrous insertion—and it expresses [the matter] with the present tense (muḍāriʿ), which indicates renewal together with continuity, because the context requires it, as was mentioned at its beginning. So it says: ﴿We insert it﴾; that is, the reminder (dhikr); ﴿into the hearts of the criminals﴾; that is, those who are deeply immersed in criminality in every age; just as a thread or a spear or the like is passed through that into which it is threaded, such as a needle or other things, with the utmost difficulty, so the place does not have room for it, and so it does not benefit them—while they are

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 13:

﴿They do not believe in it﴾; (i.e., in anything of the things); because their breasts do not expand to it; as you have seen the way of Our practice concerning that among your people; ﴿and there has already passed﴾; i.e., there has gone by before this; ﴿the way of the former peoples﴾; i.e., the custom (p-28) concerning that; and We are able to do what We wish with regard to that way with this community; such as destruction, and facilitating faith, and other than that; so it refers to His saying: ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1]; and the purpose is to explain that He (exalted be He) blinds some eyes to what is plain, and gives sight to some of them to what is hidden; to manifest power and choice, by carrying out the command contrary to what is analogically expected.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 14:

When He had informed him of these secrets, revealing their states, and the soul is most eager for anything that cuts off the argument of the obstinate by granting his request, He (Exalted is He) said, informing of the realization of what He had concluded with, namely that they do not believe in extraordinary signs, and that even if they saw something more wondrous than the coming of the angels: ﴿And even if We opened for them﴾; that is, by what We possess of greatness; ﴿upon them﴾; that is, upon those who said: "Why do you not bring us the angels?"; ﴿a gate﴾; befitting Our greatness; ﴿from the heaven﴾. And He indicated that this would be their condition, even if they were in the clearest of times, which is the daytime, by His saying: ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾; that is, the disbelievers; ﴿through it﴾; that is, through that lofty gate; ﴿ascending﴾; that is, they climb, walking upward; ﴿with the gait of joy﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 15:

﴿They would say﴾ out of obstinacy and aversion from faith: ﴿"Our eyes have only been intoxicated"﴾; that is, they have been blocked and covered over; ﴿"Our sight"﴾; that is, to the point that we imagined what is not real to be real; ﴿"Rather, we are a people"﴾; that is, even though we have the utmost strength to attempt what we wish; ﴿"bewitched"﴾; that is, the occurrence of sorcery upon us is established, to the point that we see things contrary to what they are, and affirm what has no reality.

And "al-sakr" (intoxication, blocking): the blocking of something by introducing a subtle substance into the pores, so that it prevents the thing from being in its complete state. From it comes "sukr" (intoxication) by wine. And "al-sihr" (sorcery): a hidden stratagem that gives the impression of the meaning of a miracle without reality.

When this heavenly sign was mentioned, by way of supposition, in answer to their denial of prophethood, it served as evidence of their persistence in disbelief. It is well known that the establishment of prophethood depends on the establishment of divine unity. So the attentive listener expects information about the signs of His (Exalted) that are verifiably existent and observable, which indicate His power. Therefore He followed this with proof of His unity through His created things, as an explanation of His words: ﴿that they may know that He is but one God﴾ [Ibrahim: 52]. It also serves as evidence of their failure to believe in the extraordinary. He began with the heavenly bodies, because they are apparent to everyone, because of their nobility, and because it is evident that they are extraordinary, given that no one can touch them or reach them. So He said, opening with the particle of expectation: ﴿And We have certainly placed﴾. That is, by the might that is Ours, which no one other than Us can attain, something that needs no opening of a gate or the like. ﴿in the sky constellations (buruj)﴾. That is, stations for the moon. It is the plural of burj (بُرْجٌ), which originally means a lofty palace. The first of them is Aries (al-Hamal), and the last is Pisces (al-Hut). They are so called because, for the wandering planets, they are like dwellings for their inhabitants. They differ in their natures, so the course of the sun and the moon through each of them produces an effect that the other does not produce. Their differing in this respect, although their relation to the sky is one, is evidence of one chosen Agent. The Arabs know these better than anyone, and their differences as well. The root b-r-j (بَرَجَ), in all its permutations, revolves around manifestness that necessarily entails height, which necessarily entails strength; but it may be excessive, and then weakness is entailed. From the general sense of manifestness comes the phrase "buruj of the sky." Al-Qazzaz said: they were called buruj because they are the houses of the stars, so they are, as it were, like fortresses for them. It has also been said that they were named for their height, since every lofty fortress is a burj. And al-Baraj (البَرَجُ), with a vowel on both letters: the breadth of the whiteness of the eye and the clarity of its blackness. It has also been said that al-Baraj in the eye is when the whiteness surrounds the blackness, appearing in a person's view, so that none of the blackness of the eye is hidden. Tabarrajat al-mar'ah (تَبَرَّجَتِ المَرْأةُ) means the woman displayed her charms. Al-Jirbiya' (الجِرْبِياءُ) is the north wind, because of its height. Al-Jarib (الجَرِيبُ) is a valley, because of its visibility. Al-Jarib is also a measure of four qafiz (أقْفِزَةٍ). Jarib al-ard (جَرِيبُ الأرْضِ) is a known measure, namely a square open area, each side of which is sixty cubits. From the same root comes al-jiraab (الجِرابُ), a container of leather, and al-jawrab (الجَوْرَبُ), the wrapping of the foot, because both are conspicuous in relation to what is within them. Likewise al-jurruban (الجُرُبّانُ), the sheath of a sword. Jiraab al-bi'r (جِرابُ البِئْرِ) is the interior of a well. Al-arjab (الأرْجابُ) are the intestines, by likeness to the leather container. Al-barijah (البارِجَةُ) is a warship of the sea used for fighting. Al-bujrah (البُجْرَةُ) is every knot in the belly; al-ujrah (العُجْرَةُ) is every knot in the body; al-bujrah is also the protruding navel, and the navel of a camel, whether large or not. Al-bujr and al-bujri (البُجْرُ، والبُجْرِيُّ) mean a great matter. "So-and-so came with al-bujarah (بِالبُجارَةِ)," which is a calamity. In this root is what unites manifestness with strength. From it comes Rajab (رَجَبٌ), the name of a month; rajibtu al-rajul (رَجِبْتُ الرَّجُلَ) means I magnified him; al-rujbah, applied to medicines; al-rajb means shyness and pardon; al-rajb also means awe; al-mujarrib (المُجَرِّبُ) is one who has been afflicted by hardships; rajabtu al-nakhl tarjiban (رَجَبْتُ النَّخْلَ تَرْجِيبًا) means I built a support on its side so that it would not fall. Al-jabr (الجَبْرُ) is the opposite of breaking; it also means king, because the mending of the broken is found in him through his strength. Jabartu al-'azm (جَبَرْتُ العَظْمَ) means I set the bone; al-jabbarah (الجَبارَةُ) is what is placed on a fracture so that it may be set. Jabartu al-rajul (جَبَرْتُ الرَّجُلَ) means I did him a kindness; ajbartuhu (أجْبَرْتُهُ) means I joined him to what he wanted; ajbartuhu 'ala kadha (أجْبَرْتُهُ عَلى كَذا) means I overpowered him to do it, that is, I removed his capacity to resist. Al-jarabbah (الجَرَبَّةُ) is a herd of donkeys; it also means strong people. Al-jabbar min al-nakhl (الجَبّارُ مِنَ النَّخْلِ) is the tall, vigorous palm tree. Al-Jabbar (الجَبّارُ) is one of the names of Allah (Exalted). Al-jabbar is also every tyrant, everything beyond reach of the hand, the great, strong and tall, and the proud one who sees no one as having a right over him. Al-mutajabbir (المُتَجَبِّرُ) is the lion. Jubar (جُبارٌ), with a damma and lightened, is Tuesday, because Allah (Exalted) created the disliked thing on it, as in the Sahih. From weakness comes al-jubar (الجُبارُ), with a damma and lightened, which is wasted blood, wars and other things. It may also derive from jabr al-kasr (the mending of a break), because the one whose blood is wasted is mended by it, strengthened by it, and treated well. Every thing that corrupts and destroys is a jabbar, as if it were likened to the splint which corrupts in order to set the break. Al-jabr (الجَبْرُ) is also the slave, because of his weakness and his need to be strengthened. Also from weakness is al-jarab (الجَرِبُ), with respect to the one it afflicts, though it is strength with respect to itself, and also from manifestness and spreading. Al-jarba' (الجَرْباءُ) is the sky, by likeness to the mangy one; ardun jarba' (أرْضٌ جَرْباءُ) is a barren land. Al-tarabbuj (التَّرَبُّجُ) is tyranny. Al-rawbaj (الرَّوْبَجُ) is a small dirham; al-Zubaidi said it is a loanword. The root j-b-r, in its particular ordering, revolves around benefit; at times it considers what necessarily follows from it, namely the absence of harm, as in al-jubar (الجُبارُ), with a damma and lightened, for what is wasted; and at times it considers what necessarily follows from benefit, namely haughtiness and domination.

When He mentioned the constellations, the Glorified described the sky that contains them, and said: ﴿And We have adorned it﴾. That is, the sky, because it is the one spoken of, with the stars; ﴿for the beholders﴾. That is, for everyone who has the readiness to look into the signs of divine unity, and for whom nothing prevents knowledge of that except not directing his gaze to it with sight or with insight.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 17:

﴿And We guarded it﴾; i.e., by what We have of greatness; ﴿from every devil﴾; i.e., far from good; burning; ﴿accursed﴾ (p-33) deserving of being stoned — and stoning (rajm) is the throwing of a thing by force, without an instrument prepared for hitting, such as a bow, for a bow is for shooting (ramy), not for stoning — and deserving of reviling, because he speaks by conjecture and about what has no reality;

﴿Except one who steals a hearing﴾ from among them, for We did not intend complete protection from it. ﴿Then he is pursued﴾, that is, he follows it like one who urges on his own self and drives it, ﴿by a shihab﴾, which is a column of light that extends with the intensity of its brightness, like fire, ﴿clear﴾, seen by whoever has the capacity to see when it is hurled with it.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Tafsir, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When the decree is issued in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon smooth rock. It penetrates them, and when fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth,' and He is the Most High, the Great. Then the eavesdroppers hear it, and the eavesdroppers are one above another, like this," and Sufyan described it with his hand, spreading the fingers of his right hand and placing some of them above others. "Sometimes the shihab overtakes the listener before he can throw it to his companion, and it burns him. And sometimes it does not overtake him until he throws it to the one beneath him, down to the one below him, until they cast it to the earth." Sufyan sometimes said: "until it reaches the earth." "Then it is cast upon the mouth of the sorcerer, and he lies with it a hundred lies, and then he is believed. They say: 'Did he not tell us that on such and such a day such and such would happen? And we found it true?' Because of the word that was heard from the heaven."

The exegetes (mufassirun), may Allah be pleased with them, said: The devils were not barred from the heavens, so they would convey what they heard from them to the soothsayers (kahanah). When ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was born, they were prevented from three heavens. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was born, they were prevented from all the heavens. Thus I have seen "was born" written, but perhaps it is "was sent," for it is in the Sahih (the authentic collection) that what prevented them was the descent of the Qur'an.

When he mentioned the sign of the sky, he followed it with the sign of the earth, saying: ﴿And the earth – We have spread it out﴾; i.e., by the greatness that is ours, in its three dimensions: length, breadth, and depth; upon the water; ﴿and We have cast﴾; i.e., by Our greatness; ﴿therein﴾; i.e., in the earth; ﴿firm mountains﴾; i.e., stable ones; lest it sway with its inhabitants; and so that they may serve as signs for them. Then he drew attention to the bringing of the dead back to life through what He bestowed upon the earth, by way of a clear analogy (qiyas jali), with His words: ﴿And We caused to grow therein﴾; i.e., in the earth, especially the mountains; by Our overwhelming power; ﴿of every thing weighed﴾ [p. 35], i.e., measured according to the requirement of wisdom; from minerals and plants.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 20:

﴿And We have made for you﴾; that is, as a favour from Us to you; ﴿therein means of livelihood﴾; written with a clear yā' and without a madd; the plural of "ma'ishah" (livelihood), which is that by which life is sustained, such as food, clothing, minerals, and other things; ﴿and [for] those whom you do not provide sustenance﴾; that is, O you mighty and powerful leaders; ﴿for whom you are not providers﴾; like you in that regard. We have made for them therein means of livelihood as well, [such as] dependants, servants, and all the other animals from which you benefit. Even if you think that you provide for them, that is false, because you cannot provide for your own selves, so how [could you provide] for others?! When the perfection of His power became manifest like the sun, and that He is One with no partner, He made clear that just as these things were with Him in measure, ordained by Him according to a wisdom He arranged, so too were others like that. This is what prevents Him from hastening upon them the punishment they mock, so He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 21:

﴿And there is not a thing﴾; that is, "and there is not"; ﴿of anything﴾; that is, of what has been mentioned; and of other possible things, which have no end; ﴿but with Us are its treasuries﴾; that is, by virtue of the overpowering power that We possess; ﴿its treasuries﴾; that is, as is established with you, not disputed by you; al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: the mention of "treasuries" is a figure of speech (tamthil); ﴿and We do not send it down﴾; that is, the absolute of that thing, not restricted by the condition of being non-finite; for everything that is brought forth into existence is finite; so this is a usage ﴿except in a known measure﴾; according to a gradual order, as you see it; and from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "There is no year that is wetter than another year; but Allah distributes it and determines it upon the earth however He wills: a year here, and a year there; and perhaps it is in the sea." So this is definitive proof that the agent who specifies it for one time over another time, and one land over another land, is one, a free-choosing agent.

When al-Biqa'i had completed what He willed concerning the two signs, the heavens and the earth, and concluded it with the all-encompassing extent of His power over everything, He followed it with what arises from them, which is located between them, deposited in the treasuries of His power. So He said: ﴿And We send the winds﴾; that is, by the dazzling disposal that is Ours; ﴿the winds﴾, the plural of "rih" (wind), which is a subtle body, dispersed in the atmosphere, swift in its passing; ﴿fertilizing﴾, that is, carrying, bearing moisture; then it releases it into the clouds that they produce. So they are carriers of water, attached to the atmosphere, and their strength for that is high, both sensibly and in meaning. And "al-rih" is moving air, and its movement after it was still must have a cause, and it is not the very fact of its being air, nor any of the necessary attributes of its essence; otherwise its movement would be perpetual. (p-٣٧) Therefore it is only by the moving of the single, choosing Agent. ﴿Then We send down﴾; that is, by Our majesty, by means of those clouds which the winds carry; ﴿from the sky﴾; that is, the literal sky, or its direction, or the clouds, because causes ascending through the support of a thing are sometimes traced to what is near it, sometimes to what is far, and sometimes to what is farthest; ﴿water﴾, which is a fluid, flowing substance, by which every living creature's life is sustained, being of the nature of nourishment; ﴿and We give you drink from it﴾; We made it for you as a drink. It is said "saqaituhu ma'an" (I gave him water to drink), meaning that he may drink it; and "asqaituhu" means I enabled him to have it so that he may water his livestock with it. And whoever wishes. And He, glory be to Him, negated from others what He had first affirmed for Himself, so He said: ﴿and you are not its﴾; that is, of that water; ﴿storers﴾. And "al-khazn" is placing a thing in a place prepared for keeping. Thus it is established that the one capable of it is One, the Choosing.

The root "لَقَحَ" (l-q-ḥ), in its six permutations, revolves around attachment (al-lihaq), and necessitates strength and height, sensibly or in meaning. So "al-liqah" is the name of the stallion's water, because it reaches the female and she conceives it; and "qad alqaha al-fahl al-naqah" (the stallion impregnated the she-camel); and "laqahat liqahan" (she conceived): she bore; and "al-malqūh" is what she has conceived from the stallion, that is, received; and they are "al-malaqih," meaning the embryos. (p-٣٨) And "al-liqhah" is the milch she-camel, because she is fit for a hungry one to attach to her. And "alqaha al-qawm al-nakhl" (the people pollinated the palms) and "laqqahuha," when they attached them to the male palm-spathe, hanging it on them.

"Al-qahil" is what is dry of skins, because its parts attach to one another, so it shrinks; and from it comes "shaykh qahil" (a withered old man). "Al-lahaq" is everything that has attached to something, that is, overtaken it. "Al-mulhaq" is the adopted (ad'i), because he is prepared for it, since everyone who wishes may claim him. "Al-milhaq" is the she-camel that no camel can outrun. Al-Zubaidi said in "Mukhtasar al-'Ayn": and in the qunut: "Inna 'adhabaka bil-kuffari mulhiq," with kasra; that is, lāḥiq (overtaking); a dialect form.

"Al-ḥaql" is good, unplanted-free land (al-qira'), because it is prepared for whoever attaches to it. It is also said: it is the crop when its leaves have branched; this too is from that, and from its attaching to the harvest, so it becomes like the shaved. "Al-ḥaqīl" is a plant; and "al-ḥaqīlah" is moist water, that is, the green of herbs and trees, in the intestines from it; and "al-ḥaqīlah" is the pit of the date, for the attaching of everyone who consumes it with it. "Al-ḥawqalah" is soft excrement, as if it is likened to the green plant; or because it can bend at any time, and some of its parts attach to others. "Al-ḥawqal" (p-٣٩) is the weak old man unable to marry, as if he is from it; "al-ḥawqalah" is quickness of walking; "ḥaqala al-faras" (the horse was affected) when it was hurt from eating dirt, as if it is taken from "al-ḥaql"; and "ḥawqala al-shaykh": he leaned with his hands on his waist when walking, as if for the attaching of his hands to his waist.

"Al-ḥalq" is the passage of food and drink; "ḥulūq al-arḍ" are its valleys and channels, for the attaching of waters to them, and for their resemblance to throats. "Al-ḥalq" is shaving hair with a razor, from attachment and strength. "Al-maḥāliq" are rough garments that shave the hair through their roughness. "Al-ḥāliq" is the ill-omened one who shaves his people. "Al-ḥalq" is a kind of plant whose leaves are sour, as if for the quickness of livestock's attaching to it, because it is like fruit for them. "Al-ḥalqah" is a ring without a bezel, for the attaching of its parts to one another; and from it "ḥalqat al-qawm" (the circle of the people). "Al-ḥalqah" is all weaponry; either from this, because from it come the mailed coats with rings, naming a thing by the name of its part; or from strength and abstract height, because of what follows from them. "Al-ḥalq" is abundant wealth; either from that, or from its owner's attaining his desire. "Al-ḥāliq" is the lofty mountain, for its prominence, its height, and its attaching to the air. "Al-ḥawqalah" is the long-necked flask; "ḥallaqa al-ṭā'ir" (the bird soared) rose in the air, from this. "Al-liqhah" is the crow; and "al-ḥāliq" from the vine, and the al-sharā: what hangs from it on the shoots; so it is evident in attachment. "Ḥalaqa al-ḍirʿ" (the udder ascended) when it rose to the belly and drew together; so it is from height (p-٤٠) and attachment. It is said: when its milk increases, then it is from attachment. "Taḥallaqa al-qamar" (the moon was ringed): a halo formed around it. "Ḥalaqa qaḍīb al-faras ḥalqan" (the horse's member became peeled) when it was stripped, as if it was likened to what has had its hair shaved. "Ḥayy liqāḥ" (a tribe of strength): they were never owned; as if from strength and abstract height. "Al-qalaḥ" is a yellowness that covers the teeth, so it is from attachment, together with height; and the beetle is called "aqlaḥ" from this.

Therefore, once the account of what is a cause of giving life in general had been firmly established, the soul was prepared to move from it, by analogy, to true giving of life. He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And indeed, it is We who give life﴾; that is, this attribute belongs to Us in a manner of majesty, so We give life by it to whatever We will of living beings: by the spirit of the body; and to the spirit (soul) by knowledge; and to plants by growth. Although one of these is literal and the other two are figurative, combining them is permissible. ﴿And We cause to die﴾; that is, this attribute belongs to Us, so by it We manifest of Our majesty whatever We will. ﴿And We are the Inheritors﴾; that is, the complete inheritance, when creation dies, the ones who remain after everything, just as We were when there was nothing. No one among creatures has any power to cause death or to give life. Thereby the Oneness (tawhid) and the act by free choice (al-fi'l bil-ikhtiyar) are established.

Thus, when His complete power was established by this, and the effects of power are not firm except with knowledge, He (Exalted) said: ﴿And We surely know﴾; i.e., by what We have of encompassing that is beyond capacity (mu'jizah); ﴿those of you who go forward﴾; and they are those whom We decreed to die first; so it is as if in their death they hasten to go ahead (al-taqaddum) towards it; even though he himself, and each of his family, is striving with treatment to delay it; ﴿And We surely know﴾; by Our greatness; ﴿those who come later﴾; i.e., those whose lifespans We extend, so We delay their death until they seem to be racing toward that; even though they seek to treat death by drinking poison and the like, or others treat it for them by striking them with the sword or other means. Thereby it is known with certainty that the Doer is One, who chooses; and likewise every one who goes before and every one who comes after, in any attribute other than death. The meaning according to the first is: We do not cause anyone to die before his appointed term, so do not hasten Us with the threat; and prepare to repel it if you are men, for it must surely come, since the word is not changed with Me.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 25:

When the proof of the perfection of power and the comprehensiveness of knowledge was complete, the resurrection of the dead was established with certainty, since there is no obstacle from the side of power, and wisdom requires it from the side of knowledge, for the sake of justice among the servants through recompense for good and evil. Then He (Exalted is He), emphasizing against their denial, said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾; i.e., the One who is good to you by avenging you against those who oppose you and by gladdening your eye with respect to those who contradict you; ﴿He﴾; i.e., alone; ﴿will gather them﴾; i.e., He will assemble them to the place of the Resurrection after their restoration. Al-Rummani said: its original meaning is gathering living beings to a place. Then He gave the reason for that, saying, emphasizing it because of their belief in what necessitates denial: ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise﴾; i.e., He does things in their most perfect places, such that no one can undo them; ﴿All-Knowing﴾; of perfect knowledge, so nothing is hidden from Him. And He wills that His wisdom be seen by removing the veil, at the distinguishing of the people of happiness from the people of wretchedness. And "al-hikmah" (wisdom): knowledge that restrains from what is not fitting; its original root is restraint (al-man').

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 26:**

Since it is His divine custom to mention the origin of creation as evidence for the return (resurrection), both before and after, and since here He began with mention of the gathering (ḥashr) because of the evidence He had established through the revival of the earth, the listener anticipated a detailed account of the origin of creation, which is the strongest evidence for resurrection, after its summary in His words: ﴿And indeed, We give life﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:23]. So He said, opening with the particle of anticipation (ḥarf al-tawaqqu'): ﴿And We created﴾, that is, with dazzling majesty; ﴿man﴾, that is, the one who is intimate with himself and forgetful of others; ﴿from clay of dried mud﴾ (ṣalṣāl), that is, dry clay which, when struck, produces a ṣalṣala, that is, an intense sound that reverberates in the air. If the sound has extension without reverberation, it is called ṣalal. So the meaning is clay of intense dryness, but unfired. As for what has been fired, it is pottery (fakhkhār).

Then He clarified the origin of the ṣalṣāl, saying: ﴿from black mud﴾ (ḥama'), that is, black clay, foul-smelling; ﴿molded﴾ (masnūn), that is, poured out and prepared for the making of what is intended from it by kneading and shaping, through movement, agitation, and being set in a balanced form and manner. All of this is in the utmost ease, pliability, and humility. Thus He mentioned the origin of man and what befell him from Iblīs, who is the origin of the jinn, just as Ādam (peace be upon him), the father of mankind, [befell] through guile, until he was expelled from the abode of purity to the abode of turbidity, so that the wise among the children of Ādam might beware of him.

In the indication, through the beginning of creation, that mankind arrives at an origin that came about by pure power, unlike them in their coming-into-being between two parents, and that the jinn arrive at an origin whose creation is not like theirs, there is a great admonition that existing things terminate in an existent that is not of their kind, but rather is a Creator not created, who acts by choice, is one without partner, and is not to be questioned, able to do what He wills, glorified is He. In His creating from water, which is like a father, and clay, which is like a mother, with the assistance of fire and air, there is wisdom in that it is suited to what is in this world, so that its survival is by means of that from which it was created, in its food, drink, clothing, and all its affairs. That is more indicative of the wisdom of the Creator, His knowledge, and His oneness.

The root ṣ-l-l (ṣalla) revolves around ṣalṣāl, which is clay in general, or free clay mixed with sand, or clay as long as it has not been made into pottery. All the meanings of the root branch out from it, because among its necessary qualities at its beginning is water, and softness through its moisture and its ease of mixing with other things; hence concealment arises, since it is pierced without sound. Among them is the acceptance of purification from adulteration. Among them, at its end, is hardness due to intense dryness, so the parts necessarily cohere and become compressed in an orderly or disorderly arrangement; and there is sound, and intense separation through cracking. Among its necessary qualities is alteration by foulness, so there arise corruption and decay. Among its necessary qualities is intense intermingling, such that when something lodges in it, it is difficult to extract. Among its necessary qualities is its distinctness from what is other than it, and a place in which it is fashioned.

From sound and dryness: ṣalīl al-ḥadīd (the ringing of iron), and of camels, and the like. It is said: ṣalla al-ḥadīd wa-l-liǧām, meaning its sound extended. If the reverberation of the sound is imagined, it is said ṣalṣala. And ṣalla al-bayḍ (the eggs) means a resonance was heard upon tapping. And al-mismār ṣalīlan means the nail was struck and so it was made to enter the thing with difficulty. And al-ibil ṣalīlan means the camels' intestines dried from thirst, so a sound was heard from them upon drinking.

From sound: ṣalṣala means he threatened and menaced, and killed the commander of the army, because of the spread of fame through that. And ṣalṣala al-ra'd means its sound became pure. And ṣalṣala al-kalima means he uttered the word in an affected manner. And ṣalṣal is a bird, or the turtledove (fākhita); and the skilled shepherd. And al-muṣallil, like muḥaddith, means the noble lord of high lineage and pure descent, and the cobbler (askaf), which is the iskāf in common usage. And taṣalṣala al-ghadīr means its mud dried out, so its dryness became ready to make a sound. And al-ḥulī ṣawwata (the ornament made a sound). And ḥimār ṣulṣul and ṣulāṣil, with both vowelled with ḍamma; and ṣalṣāl and muṣalṣil, meaning making a sound.

From foulness: ṣulūl al-laḥm wa-l-mā' (the rotting of meat and water). It is said: ṣalla al-laḥm ṣulūlan, meaning it became foul; and the water became stagnant. And al-ṣilliyān, with two kasras and the lām doubled, means what has changed in meat. And al-ṣulla, with ḍamma, means the foul-smelling wind.

From dryness: al-ṣilla, which is dry hide before tanning, and the sandal, and the ground, or dry land. And ṣalla al-siqā' ṣalīlan means the waterskin dried out; or a land that was not rained upon between two rainfalls. And al-ṣill, with kasra, means a horn, a tree, and a cutting sword. From moisture: al-ṣilla, which is moist earth. From water, more general than whether it is abundant or little: al-ṣilla is for a wide rain and for scattered little rain. And al-ṣulla, with ḍamma, is the remnant of water or other things; likewise ṣalṣala and ṣalṣal, both vowelled with ḍamma, mean the remnant of water in the pool, and likewise of grease and oil. As for dispersal, it comes from cracking. And al-ṣila is a piece of herbage, named after rain, naming the cause by the name of its cause. From softness: al-ṣalāla, with kasra, is the lining of a boot, or its shank. And al-ṣulṣul, like hudhud, is the forelock of a horse, and it may be pronounced with fatḥa; or whiteness in the hair of its mane, and what has whitened of the hair of its back. This is also from distinctness. From the place: a cup, or its small one. And al-miṣla, with kasra, is a vessel in which drink is strained. From foulness: al-ṣill, with kasra, is a snake in general, or the thin yellow one, and the calamity, and the cutting sword; it is likened to these because of its destruction. And innahu la-ṣullu aṣlāl means he is a calamity, an objectionable person in disputes and otherwise. And ṣalathumu al-ṣāllatu means the calamity befell them; and this too is from intense intermingling. From cracking: al-ṣāll, which is water that falls on the ground so that it cracks. From purification: ṣallalnā al-ḥabba al-mukhtalaṭa bi-l-turāb means we poured water upon it, so we separated each thing from the other. And ṣalla al-sharāb ṣalλan means he strained the drink. And al-miṣla, with kasra, is the vessel in which it is strained. From the compression and constriction of parts, which may occur with or without order: from it is talṣīṣ al-bunyān, meaning its consolidation; and order is not necessarily required in it. From it is al-taṣṣ, in the sense of sticking. And al-laṣṣ, which is the closeness of the two shoulders and the closeness of the molars, and the pressing of a horse's two elbows toward its chest. And al-laṣṣā' from foreheads means narrow; and a woman whose thighs cling together, with no gap between them; and a black man with tight buttocks; and the closing of a door. From its application to what is not orderly even without closeness: al-laṣṣā' min al-ghanam, which is the one whose one horn faces forward and the other turns back. From concealment, which is a necessary quality of clay while it is moist: al-laṣṣ, with fatḥa, which is doing a thing in concealment, and the thief; it may also be pronounced with three vowels.

The root s-n-n (sanna) revolves around rubbing, and necessarily entails beautification. From rubbing: al-sinn, with kasra, which is the molar; a clove of garlic, which is likened to it; the wild bull; the spearhead; the place of the pen's slit; intense eating; the horn; the blade of a sickle; and the measure of a lifespan, because when it passes over its companion it is as though it rubbed him. And al-masānn of camels are the large ones. And sunn al-sikkīn (the blade of the knife) and other things; so it is masnūn. And al-misann, with kasra, is the instrument of sharpening. And sanna rumḥahu ilayhi means he aimed it at him. And sanna al-aḍrās means he cleaned the teeth with a siwāk. And sanna al-ibil means he drove the camels quickly, because they rub against each other when crowded. And sanna al-amr means he clarified it, as though he prepared it to be ridden, so that it is rubbed by thoughts or other things. And sanna al-ṭīn means he made it into pottery. And sanna fulānan means he stabbed him with a spearhead or bit him with teeth. And al-faḥl sanna al-nāqa means the stallion threw the she-camel on her face. And ʿalayhi al-dir' aw al-mā' means he poured it upon him, the armor or the water. And al-ṭarīqa means he traveled it. And istann means he used the siwāk. And al-faras means it kicked. And al-sarāb means it shook. And al-sinna, with kasra, is an axe with two heads. And al-sunna, with ḍamma, is conduct or disposition, as though it had been worked on until it became submissive. And al-sunna from God is His judgment, His command and His prohibition. And sunan al-ṭarīq, with three vowels or with two ḍammas, is its course and direction. And jā'at al-rīḥ sanāsin means it came in one manner. And al-ḥama' al-masnūn means the foul one, because it was made ready to be rubbed by the tool, in its formation, until it became suitable for what it is used for. And al-faḥl yusānn al-nāqa means he bites her, and drives her, until he makes her kneel to mate with her. And al-sanīn, like amīr, means what falls from the stone when you scrape it; and the land whose plants have been eaten is like the masnūna. And al-sinsin, with kasra, means thirst, as though it had scorched the intestines until it burned them; and the head of the pulley, that is, the great wheel; and the vertebra of the spine; like al-sann and al-sansana; and the head of the chest bones, or the end of the rib in the chest. And al-mustasann is the traveled road; and al-mustann is the lion; and al-sanan, with movement, means the camels that gallop in their running. And al-sanīna, like safīna, means the high, elongated sand upon the face of the earth; and it is from al-masnūn in the sense of poured. And sannanī hādhā al-shay' means it made the food desirable to me, as though it sharpened the stomach until it was cut after its weariness. And tasannat al-fuḥūl means they bit one another. And al-nass means swiftness of going, and it entails the rubbing of the limbs. And nasīs al-insān means his exertion, because that happens only after the most intense agitation. And al-nasīsa means the remnant of life, which is the remnant of the spirit of the sick and the wounded, as though it were struck until most of it departed. And nassa al-laḥm means its moisture departed from the intensity of cooking, because the burning of fire is the greatest rubbing. Likewise nassa al-ḥaṭab, when the fire brings out its foam on its head, because the burning takes the place of crushing in what its oil is extracted from. And nassa min al-ʿaṭash means he dried out. From this also comes, from beautification: sannana al-manṭiq, when he made speech beautiful; and sanna al-amr means he clarified it; and al-ṭīn means he made it into pottery; and al-māl means he sent it out to graze, or he tended it well, until it was as though he polished it; and al-shay' means he shaped it. And al-sunna, with ḍamma, means the face, or its heat, or its circle, or the form, or the forehead. And rajul masnūn al-wajh means smoothed, beautiful, easy, or there is length in his face and nose. All of this also returns to rubbing. And God knows best.

And Abū Ḥayyān said: Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: al-masnūn is the moist one; its meaning is the poured, because it is not poured unless it is moist. And al-Rāzī said in al-Lawāmiʿ: This is an indication of the stages of the creation of Ādam, peace be upon him, and its levels; and Allah (exalted is He) indicated this in various places, as wisdom required. So He said in one place: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:59], indicating the first beginning; and in another: ﴿from clay﴾ [al-Mu'minūn 23:12], indicating the combination of water and dust; and in another: ﴿from black mud molded﴾, indicating changed clay, settled in a state of balance fit to receive form; and in another: ﴿from dried clay﴾, indicating its dryness and the hearing of a sound from it; and in another: ﴿from dried clay like pottery﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:14], which is that which has been put right by a trace of fire, so that it became like baked clay. And by this fiery power there came about in man a trace of satanic nature. End.

And al-Rummānī said: The verses have included the explanation of what the alteration of the animal from one state to another necessitates, from a capable Maker who transformed it from a source that is farthest of all things from the state of an animal, into an animal. He said: The wisdom in His making it from black mud lies in the lesson that it was transformed from that lowly state in quality into this noble state.

When He mentioned the creation of man, He (glory be to Him) followed it with mention of what He created before him from the jinn. So He said: ﴿And the jann﴾; that is, the one who belongs to the jinn, as Adam (peace be upon him) belongs to mankind. It was said that this is Iblis. ﴿We created him﴾. He expressed the shortness of the time between his creation and that of man, and its nearness, by using the preposition ﴿from before﴾ (min qabl). That is, before the creation of man. ﴿From the fire of the samum﴾; that is, the intense heat. It was said that it is a fire without smoke, from which lightning bolts come. It lies between the sky and the veil. When God (exalted be He) wills, it tears through the veil and strikes what it is commanded to strike. The crash that people hear is the tearing of that veil. Al-Razi said in *al-Lawami'*: it is a subtle fire that has reached extreme boiling in the horizon of the air. Compared with the fire that God (exalted be He) made a provision, like ice compared with water and stone compared with dust, it is subtle. End of quotation. Abdullah said: this samum is one part of seventy parts of the samum from which God created the jann. It is derived from its entering the pores of the body with its subtlety, and from it comes the word *summ* (poison), which kills. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 15, verse 28:

When the blessing of creation (ni'mat al-ijad) was sufficient to make worship sincere toward the One who brought things into being, and the people of misguidance nonetheless did not take heed of it, (Exalted is He) pointed to a blessing greater than it, namely the preferring of (Adam) over all created beings, in a manner that clarifies the cause of misguidance.
